question: Inhibin: a new circulating marker of hydatidiform mole?
answer: In patients with newly diagnosed complete hydatidiform mole, serum inhibin was significantly higher before evacuation (median 8.3 U/ml) than in normal pregnant women at the same stage (2.8 U/ml), and it fell significantly within 7-10 days of evacuation to follicular-phase levels (0.4 U/ml). This supports inhibin as a circulating marker of mole. Molar tissue itself contained high inhibin concentrations (median cytosol 578 U/ml), consistent with the mole being a source of circulating inhibin. None of the four patients whose post-evacuation serum inhibin was 0.4 U/ml or less developed persistent trophoblastic disease, suggesting possible prognostic value. In a mixed series of trophoblastic tumours, inhibin A was raised in 10/17 patients and inhibin B in 4/17, while HCG and HCGbeta were high in all. Inhibin A tracked HCG during chemotherapy and normalized faster than HCG in some patients, whereas inhibin B did not correlate with HCGbeta.

question: Vertical lines in distal esophageal mucosa (VLEM): a true endoscopic manifestation of esophagitis in children?
answer: In a retrospective review of pediatric esophageal biopsies, VLEM as the only endoscopic abnormality was associated with histologic esophagitis: only 1 of 41 biopsies (2.4%) in the VLEM group was histologically normal, versus 57.5% of biopsies from endoscopically normal mucosa. question: Does the SCL 90-R obsessive-compulsive dimension identify cognitive impairments?
answer: In 19 adults with malignant brain tumors, the SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was not related to objective measures of attention or verbal memory, so it did not identify objectively measured cognitive impairment. The subscale was instead strongly related to depression (r = .81), anxiety (r = .66), and subjective memory complaints (r = .75). Depression accounted for 66% of the variance in subscale scores and anxiety for an additional 6%, suggesting it mainly reflects mood symptoms and perceived memory problems.

question: Hypotension in patients with coronary disease: can profound hypotensive events cause myocardial ischaemic events?

question: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
answer: In a prospective study of 224 IVF patients, baseline antral follicle count >6 was associated with a much higher clinical pregnancy rate than count ≤6 (51% vs 19%), and this held after controlling for patient age and basal FSH. question: Is eligibility for a chemotherapy protocol a good prognostic factor for invasive bladder cancer after radical cystectomy?
answer: In a single-institution comparison after radical cystectomy, patients eligible for and entered into the SAKK 09/84 adjuvant chemotherapy protocol had better outcomes than matched and remaining non-protocol patients. question: Can bedside assessment reliably exclude aspiration following acute stroke?
answer: In a prospective study of 94 acute stroke patients against videofluoroscopy, bedside assessment by a speech and language therapist had only 47% sensitivity (NPV 85%), and aspiration went undetected at the bedside in 10 of the 20 patients who were aspirating, so it could not reliably exclude aspiration. The best combination of bedside elements (weak voluntary cough plus any alteration in conscious level) reached 75% sensitivity and 91% NPV, but specificity was 72% and PPV 41%, so some aspiration would still be missed. Another prospective study (121 patients) found that bedside dysphagia assessment was associated with outcomes such as chest infection and mortality, and that videofluoroscopy added no value to bedside assessment for detecting aspiration. This concerns prognostic value rather than the accuracy of excluding aspiration. Pulse oximetry, a bedside adjunct, predicted aspiration or its absence correctly in 81.5% of 54 dysphagic stroke patients, but its predictive value was low in patients aged 65 or older and possibly in those with chronic lung disease, with a false negative in one smoker.

question: Is laparoscopic adrenalectomy safe and effective for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm?

question: Body diffusion-weighted MR imaging of uterine endometrial cancer: is it helpful in the detection of cancer in nonenhanced MR imaging?
answer: Adding diffusion-weighted (DW) images to nonenhanced T2-weighted MR imaging improved detection of endometrial cancer, raising sensitivity from 83% (19/23) with T2-weighted images alone to 96% when DW and fused DW/T2-weighted images were added. question: Does a colonoscopy after acute diverticulitis affect its management?
answer: In a retrospective review of 220 patients hospitalized for acute diverticulitis, early (4-6 week) colonoscopy in 100 patients detected no colonic malignancy and led to no new or different diagnosis, suggesting it did not change management. By contrast, the CFH polymorphism rs1061170 was associated with AMD: carrying at least one C allele raised risk independent of age (OR 2.42, 95% CI 1.22-4.81), while the ancestral T allele was protective (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.34-0.83). The SKIV2L (rs429608) and MYRIP (rs2679798) polymorphisms also showed no significant difference between AMD patients and controls.

question: Does radiotherapy of the primary rectal cancer affect prognosis after pelvic exenteration for recurrent rectal cancer?
answer: In a retrospective review of 87 patients undergoing pelvic exenteration for locally recurrent rectal cancer, prior radiotherapy for the primary tumour was associated with worse prognosis, including lower disease-free survival (p = 0.022). Previously irradiated patients required more radical exenterations (68% vs 44%), had lower rates of clear resection margins (63% vs 87%), and had more surgical complications per patient. Among patients with clear margins, overall and disease-free survival were still lower in the primarily irradiated group, and the survival difference persisted in multivariate analysis adjusting for primary tumour T and N stage.

question: Rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane: is partial prostatectomy oncologically adequate?
answer: In a retrospective multicentre series of 126 men with rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane, partial prostatectomy after preoperative chemoradiotherapy gave a free anterior circumferential resection margin in all cases, and the overall CRM-positive rate after chemoradiotherapy plus prostatic resection was 2.4%. Without preoperative chemoradiotherapy, CRM positivity was much higher: 25.0% when the prostatic plane was threatened and 41.7% when it was affected. With preoperative radiotherapy the rates were 7.1% and 20.7%, respectively. Oncological adequacy was achieved at a surgical cost: intra-operative urethral damage occurred in 36.4% of patients undergoing partial prostatectomy, and a postoperative urinary fistula developed in 18.2%. Margin status matters for outcome in locally advanced rectal cancer: after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, local recurrence was 10% with R0 resection versus 62% with R1-R2 resection, and survival was worse with a positive CRM.

question: Literacy after cerebral hemispherectomy: Can the isolated right hemisphere read?

question: Preparing patients at high risk of falls for discharge home after rehabilitation: Do we meet the guidelines?
answer: A retrospective audit of 50 high-falls-risk patients discharged home after inpatient rehabilitation found guideline-concordant preparation was incomplete: discharge documentation correctly identified falls risk for only 9 of 50 patients. Patients at high falls risk had a median of 8 of 17 risk factors, but assessment of some factors was rarely documented: osteoporosis (n=8), footwear (n=4), and visual assessment in the previous 2 years (n=1). Patients received a median of 6.5 of 16 possible falls prevention strategies, with mobility (n=48), strength (n=44), and Personal Activity of Daily Living training (n=43) the most common. Practice was better for strategy implementation once a risk factor was identified: for 12 risk factors, a strategy was documented in more than 80% of records when the factor was present.

question: Could chest wall rigidity be a factor in rapid death from illicit fentanyl abuse?
answer: Post-mortem data from 48 fentanyl deaths suggest chest wall rigidity could contribute to rapid death: no measurable norfentanyl was found in about half of cases (42% none detected, 52% under 1 ng/ml), which the authors interpret as very rapid death consistent with acute chest rigidity. Fentanyl concentrations did not track with norfentanyl levels, and some deaths had strikingly high fentanyl (20-22 ng/ml) with no norfentanyl detected. Other deaths occurred at low, therapeutic-range fentanyl levels (1-2 ng/ml) in apparent non-naïve opioid users. The authors link the surge in deaths to a change in route of administration, since rapid intravenous fentanyl can produce chest wall rigidity. They note that this complication is well recognized in medicine but unknown within the drug-abusing community, who may be unaware of rising fentanyl content in illicit opioids.

question: Do risk calculators accurately predict surgical site occurrences?

question: Are serum leptin levels a prognostic factor in advanced lung cancer?
answer: In 71 previously untreated lung cancer patients, serum leptin levels showed no association with overall survival, so leptin did not behave as a prognostic factor in this study. Leptin levels were also not significantly related to clinicopathological parameters such as ECOG performance status, weight loss, histological type, disease stage or TNM classification, although they correlated with BMI. Serum leptin was significantly lower in lung cancer patients than in matched controls, which reflects a diagnostic or association difference rather than prognostic value.
